lead: The Word of God was not given as knowledge for human beings to use in condemning and controlling one another, but as the living Word that leads us to love God and love our neighbour. This study follows a single biblical trajectory through the Torah, religious power, God who came as man, the Church in an age of expanding knowledge, and the return of Yeshua, arguing that the centre of Christian hope must remain the Lord who is coming again.

blocks.text: Scripture quotations are from the King James Version (KJV).
1. The Essence of the Torah and Israel
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full.
Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. / Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.

The first principle we must establish when interpreting the Bible is that Scripture was written through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit of God. The prophets and biblical writers of both the Old and New Testaments lived in different periods and circumstances, yet their testimony ultimately points to God and to Yeshua, God who came in human flesh. Therefore, rather than reading the Bible merely as a collection of separate religious documents, we should understand it within the great and continuous movement of God progressively revealing Himself, His will, and His work of salvation.

Before turning to Yeshua who came as a man, however, we must first consider Israel. God chose a people to whom He would entrust His Word and His covenant. They were Israel, the descendants of Jacob and the children of Abraham. Before entering the land of Canaan, Israel endured a long period of slavery and oppression in Egypt. God waited until the iniquity of the peoples of Canaan had reached its fullness. When the appointed time came, He used Israel as an instrument of judgment and brought them into the land.

Yet a profound irony emerges in biblical history. Israel, which had once been used as an instrument of judgment against other nations, eventually fell into the same sins as those nations and at times committed even greater evil. The people who had once participated in God’s judgment eventually became the objects of His judgment themselves. In earlier periods they suffered oppression from surrounding peoples such as the Philistines. Later, as their sin deepened and the time of divine discipline and judgment came, Israel and Judah suffered national catastrophe through Assyria and Babylon.

Although the exiles eventually returned, they subsequently lived under Persian rule, endured Greek domination and persecution, and in the New Testament period lived under Roman power. Eventually, they even experienced expulsion from their own land. Israel’s history therefore demonstrates that being chosen by God does not constitute an exemption from judgment. Rather, those who have received God’s Word bear an even greater responsibility to live in accordance with it.

When Israel entered Canaan and became a national community, it required a law by which that community could be governed. Israel was not merely an ethnic community but a covenant people called to worship God and live under His rule. The law given to them was the Torah, through which God’s government was expressed in concrete form. Using a modern legal analogy, the Ten Commandments may be compared to constitutional principles because they functioned as foundational norms, while the more specific commands and ordinances contained in the Torah may be compared to statutes or positive laws. This does not mean that the Torah is identical to a modern legal system. The comparison simply helps us understand how God governed the covenant community of Israel.

God’s justice and righteousness are revealed through this law. Yet we must not reduce the Torah to a system concerned only with prohibitions and punishments. Yeshua summarized its heart as love for God and love for one’s neighbour, declaring that upon these commandments hang all the law and the prophets. Therefore, within God’s law we find not only righteousness and justice, but also mercy, compassion, forgiveness, and care for others.

God did not desire religious ceremony alone. He desired mercy, and He placed obedience above outward sacrifice. However carefully a person may observe religious regulations, if mercy and obedience are absent, that person can still depart from the intention of the God who gave the law.

Holiness likewise means more than outward compliance with rules. To be holy is to turn away from sin, refuse to live according to the desires of the flesh, and live according to the Word of God so that one increasingly reflects God’s character. To live according to the Torah, therefore, is not merely to comply mechanically with regulations. It is to live in a manner consistent with the will and character of God.

Human beings, however, easily lose sight of this fundamental purpose of the law. When that happens, the law may cease to function as the Word of God that exposes our own condition and calls us to repentance. Instead, it can become a means of concealing our sin and displaying our own righteousness. A person may hide behind the law, present himself as righteous and religiously strict, and use that position to judge and condemn others.

Then love for God and neighbour, mercy, compassion, forgiveness, and care for the weak gradually disappear, while severity and judgment remain. The problem is not the Torah itself. The problem arises when human beings lose the heart of the God who gave the Torah and turn His law into an instrument of self-righteousness or power.
2. When the Word Becomes an Instrument of Power
For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men’s shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers.
Woe unto you, lawyers! for ye have taken away the key of knowledge: ye entered not in yourselves, and them that were entering in ye hindered.
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men...

Throughout Israel’s history, we repeatedly see a pattern of sin, judgment, crying out to God, and deliverance. During the period of the Judges, when the people departed from God they fell under oppression. When they cried out, God raised up judges to deliver them. As foreign domination continued and national independence disappeared, Israel’s longing for a Messiah naturally intensified. They hoped for a deliverer like the judges of old and for a king like David who could rescue the nation from oppression and restore it. Their expectation of the Messiah therefore became intertwined with the hope that God Himself would once again deliver His people.
Yet there is another irony. At the very time when the people most deeply longed for the Messiah, serious corruption could also be found within segments of the religious leadership.

This does not mean that every priest, Pharisee, scribe, or teacher of the law was evil. There were certainly people who genuinely feared God and faithfully awaited His Messiah. We must therefore avoid reducing all first-century Judaism to a single corrupt group. What the Gospels repeatedly expose, however, is the danger that arises when religious office and knowledge of Scripture become intertwined with institutional power.

The priests possessed religious authority connected with the Temple and its sacrifices. The scribes and teachers of the law had considerable authority in the study, interpretation, teaching, and transmission of the Torah. These responsibilities were originally intended to teach God’s will and guide people toward Him. Yet whenever knowledge is joined to entrenched privilege, knowledge itself can become a form of power.

Those who possess power face the temptation to interpret law in ways that preserve their own authority and the existing order rather than seek the will of God. Human interpretation and tradition can accumulate over generations until they begin to function almost as though they possess the same authority as the Word of God itself. Numerous interpretations and detailed regulations developed around matters such as Sabbath observance, including what could be done, what could not be done, and under what circumstances something became a violation.

The existence of interpretation or tradition is not itself the problem. The problem begins when such interpretations cease to guide people toward God and instead become burdens too heavy for them to bear.

The Torah was given by God for life and holiness and as an expression of His rule. Yet when human structures of power take control of God’s Word, a law intended for life can be transformed into an instrument of control. Knowledge that should lead people to God may instead be used to suppress, judge, and dominate them. This is precisely the problem Yeshua exposed when He rebuked those who possessed the “key of knowledge” but neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter.

We must therefore remember that knowing a great deal about Scripture is not necessarily the same thing as knowing the heart of the God who gave Scripture. In fact, the greater our knowledge becomes, the easier it may be to assume that we understand God better than others and then use that knowledge to classify, judge, and condemn them. When knowledge loses love and mercy, the very knowledge that should open the way to God can become a barrier preventing people from approaching Him.
3. God Who Came as Man
Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
He that hath seen me hath seen the Father; and how sayest thou then, Shew us the Father?

It was into such a world that God came as man. Yeshua proclaimed the kingdom of God, healed the sick, received sinners, remained among the poor and the excluded, and demonstrated mercy, compassion, and forgiveness through His actions. At the same time, He never treated sin as though it were insignificant. He confronted sin while restoring the sinner. He upheld God’s righteousness and holiness while simultaneously revealing God’s mercy.

To those who held established religious authority, what Yeshua was doing was more than an abstract theological disagreement. It could be perceived as a fundamental challenge to their authority to interpret Scripture and to the religious order over which they presided.

The problem was not that they knew nothing about Scripture. Many of them had devoted their lives to studying it, teaching the Torah, and seeking to understand the will of God. Yet once knowledge becomes hardened into an inflexible system, people can find it difficult to accept God when He acts outside the boundaries of what they have come to expect.

Political and religious power also intersected during this period. Herod the Great undertook the massive expansion of the Jerusalem Temple, a place that carried enormous religious, social, and political significance in Jewish society. His son Herod Antipas, by contrast, is the Herod whom the Gospel of Luke describes as wanting to see Yeshua personally because he had heard many things about Him and hoped to witness some miracle performed by Him.

This reveals another danger. People may desire a sign rather than God Himself. Their primary concern may become what miracle they can see or what benefit they can receive, rather than whether God Himself has come among His people.

A similar problem appears in the reaction to Yeshua’s forgiveness of sins. When He forgave sins, religious observers asked, “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” That question reaches the very heart of the matter. If only God can forgive sins, then the proper question should have been, “Who, then, is this One standing before us who claims and exercises the authority to forgive sins?”

Yet if protecting an existing theological framework becomes more important than discovering who Yeshua truly is, the same question can become not a doorway to revelation but a basis for condemning Him as a blasphemer.

The account of the woman caught in adultery in the Gospel of John presents a similar pattern. The accusers appealed to the law in order to condemn the woman, while Yeshua told them that the one without sin should cast the first stone. Yet He did not declare that her sin was irrelevant. He ultimately instructed her to sin no more.

Yeshua therefore did not deny the seriousness of sin. He revealed what divine mercy looks like when it confronts sin while seeking to restore the sinner. He did not remove justice and leave only love, nor did He remove love and leave only judgment. Righteousness and mercy, truth and compassion, appeared together.

Thus something extraordinary occurred. Among those who most eagerly awaited God and most diligently studied His Word, some failed to recognize Him when God actually came among them in human flesh. The God they expected did not correspond to the One speaking and acting before their eyes. They could wait for God within Scripture, doctrine, and tradition, yet when God acted beyond the boundaries of the system they had constructed, they could not receive Him.

This is not a story told merely to condemn people who lived two thousand years ago. It should function as a mirror for us today. We too can possess extensive biblical knowledge, theology, and doctrine, yet reject what God is doing when it falls outside our existing assumptions. More important than accumulating knowledge about the Bible is coming to know, through the Bible, the God who speaks through it.
4. The Church in an Age of Expanding Knowledge
For we know in part, and we prophesy in part.
For laying aside the commandment of God, ye hold the tradition of men...

We are living in an age in which knowledge is expanding at an extraordinary rate. Materials that were once difficult to obtain can now be accessed with relative ease. Historical documents can be compared, languages can be studied more deeply, and ancient manuscripts, archaeological evidence, and cultural backgrounds can be examined together. Biblical study has therefore entered an environment in which many assumptions inherited from earlier generations can be re-examined in light of a much broader range of evidence.

For this reason, the Church should not treat every interpretation as absolute merely because it has been transmitted for a long time. Age does not automatically make a tradition true, and widespread acceptance does not automatically make an interpretation correct. Even doctrines that have been accepted for centuries should be reconsidered if there are legitimate reasons to examine whether they truly correspond to the whole witness of Scripture.

The Protestant Reformation opened an enormously important path by returning Scripture to ordinary believers and encouraging people to read the Bible directly. Yet this also created another possibility. Individuals could interpret Scripture according to their own assumptions and produce increasingly diverse systems of doctrine. Numerous denominations and theological traditions developed, and some interpretations may have elevated particular passages or human systems beyond what Scripture itself warrants.

Yet this is not a Protestant problem alone. Catholic, Orthodox, Messianic Jewish, and every other community in which human beings interpret Scripture remain subject to the limitations of human understanding.

This does not mean that the Church throughout history has simply been wrong. Despite the limitations of human institutions, theological systems, and interpretations, God has not abandoned His Church. He continues to work among His people and care for them. Precisely because our knowledge is partial, we need one another. No individual knows everything, and no single denomination possesses the entirety of God’s truth. We need to share what we have learned, listen to one another, and allow Scripture to correct and supplement our limitations.

One example can be found among some Messianic Jewish communities that interpret the Torah’s prohibition of images very strictly and therefore hesitate to create visual representations of Yeshua or biblical scenes. Their desire to take God’s command seriously and guard against idolatry deserves respect.

At the same time, whether creating an image is identical in every respect to worshipping that image as God is a separate interpretive question. Christians and Jewish believers have understood such commandments in different ways. Rather than making one interpretation absolute here, this is an area in which believers should continue to examine Scripture carefully and humbly.

A deeper issue concerns the way we respond to visible social conditions. When a serious social phenomenon finally becomes obvious, it may indicate that something deeper had already begun to collapse before the outward symptoms appeared. Spiritual foundations may weaken first, while social and moral consequences emerge later.

For example, when a political ideology or social movement spreads rapidly, our first instinct may be to oppose the people or groups associated with it. Yet before simply attempting to remove the visible phenomenon, we should ask what has already weakened within the community itself. We should examine truth, justice, responsibility, love, integrity, and trust. Eliminating a visible symptom does not necessarily remove the underlying causes that produced it.

The same principle applies to sexual disorder and moral decline. People may begin protesting, legislating, or trying to restrain such developments only after they become highly visible. Yet before those visible conditions emerged, values such as purity, self-control, responsibility, fidelity, and holiness may already have weakened within individuals, families, churches, and society.

The spiritual foundation may collapse before the external consequences become obvious. Yet human beings often respond only after the outward phenomenon appears, relying primarily upon external force and physical action to stop what has already developed.

The Church is not exempt from this problem. When those who possess biblical knowledge use that knowledge not to lead people toward God but to protect doctrines, traditions, institutions, or personal authority, the same pattern condemned by Yeshua among certain religious leaders can arise again.

This does not mean that doctrine and tradition are inherently wrong. Doctrine is necessary for understanding Scripture systematically, and traditions may preserve valuable wisdom accumulated by communities of faith over many generations. The problem begins when doctrine and tradition cease to serve as tools for understanding Scripture and instead become absolute standards by which Scripture and even God Himself are judged.
The danger arises when we attempt to confine God within the theological system we have constructed.

We are not complete in our knowledge. We know in part. Acknowledging this does not mean abandoning truth or embracing relativism. Rather, it means possessing enough humility not to identify our own interpretation with God Himself.

The Church of God is greater than the knowledge of any one person, denomination, or theological system. The Church in which the Holy Spirit moves is greater than the boundaries human beings have constructed. Therefore, while holding firmly to truth, we must recognize our need for one another and build one another up through the understanding, gifts, and insight that God has distributed among the members of His body.
5. The Lord Is Coming
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord.
If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.

Today many believers are deeply interested in the rapture. Yet before discussing the rapture, we must first examine where the centre of our faith lies. If our primary concern becomes, “When will I be taken up?” then without realizing it, we ourselves can become the centre of the doctrine rather than the Lord.
The central message of Christ’s return, however, is not primarily about where I will go. The central truth is that the Lord is coming. Yeshua is coming again.

There are various theological interpretations concerning whether the Lord comes first in the air and then to the earth, whether tribulation precedes or follows the gathering of the saints, and how a period commonly described as seven years should be understood. These questions have produced considerable theological debate. Yet before constructing detailed prophetic timelines, one fact must remain central. Yeshua is coming again.

Paul writes that the Lord Himself will descend from heaven, that the dead in Christ will rise first, and that afterward those who remain alive will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. The centre of the passage is therefore not simply that believers are “caught up.” The Lord comes first, the dead in Christ are raised, and the living saints are gathered to meet Him.
The first question concerning the rapture should therefore not be, “When will I go up?” but, “Do I truly long for the coming of the Lord?”

We need to distinguish between longing for Yeshua and simply longing to escape from a difficult world. When the rapture is understood mainly as an escape from suffering, Christian hope can gradually become a form of spiritual withdrawal. The world is becoming darker, tribulation is coming, and therefore I simply want to leave before it becomes worse.
But Scripture does not call us to disconnect from the world and wait passively for an escape. We are called to carry the cross entrusted to each of us while we live in this world.

The cross does not merely mean enduring occasional inconvenience or hardship. The cross means death. It means denying ourselves, surrendering our own will, accepting the sacrifice and obedience entrusted to us, and following Yeshua faithfully to the end.

Each of us has a portion to carry. We cannot avoid the cross that has been entrusted to us while merely waiting for the rapture. Waiting for the Lord cannot be separated from carrying our cross and following Him today.

Scripture also contains passages showing that within God’s plan there are forms of fullness or completion yet to be reached. Revelation 6:11 speaks of the martyrs being told to rest for a little season until their fellow servants and brethren who would also be killed should be fulfilled. Ephesians speaks of believers coming “unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ.”

These passages should not be turned into mathematical formulas for predicting the date of the Second Coming. Nevertheless, they remind us that God is bringing His purpose toward a fullness and maturity determined by Him.

A community waiting for the Lord should therefore not be merely a group of people waiting to escape into heaven. It should be a people growing toward the maturity the Lord desires. Scripture speaks of the armies that accompany the returning King and of the saints reigning with Christ. The return of Yeshua should therefore be understood not merely as an individual escape from the earth but within the far greater reality of the coming kingdom and the manifestation of God’s rule.
At the same time, we must guard against another error. Spiritual maturity must not be interpreted as though we could perfect our own righteousness through human effort.

No matter how intensely religious we become, religious effort itself cannot make us righteous before God. If religious discipline alone were the standard, there are people within Judaism who observe religious regulations with extraordinary strictness, Muslims who demonstrate remarkable devotion, and adherents of other religions who practise fasting, asceticism, prayer, and discipline with extraordinary commitment.
The centre of Christian faith is not human religious achievement. We live by grace.
Yet living by grace does not mean living carelessly. To live by grace means that Yeshua is Lord. He comes first. He is the centre. We are those who follow Him.
For this reason, our understanding of the rapture and the return of Christ must begin not with the statement, “I will go up,” but with the confession, “The Lord is coming.”

The Lord comes to us, and we wait for Him. We do not approach Him carrying our own standards and demanding that He accept us according to our judgment. We will stand before Him according to His judgment and His standard.

Therefore, before judging others, we need to examine ourselves honestly. When we look deeply into our own hearts, we know how weak we are, how many faults we possess, and how easily we fall into sin. We know the desires, pride, hatred, selfishness, and other things hidden within us that other people cannot see.
We do not stand before God because we have made ourselves clean. That is why we need the grace and mercy of the Lord.

We are not people who stand before God trusting in our own righteousness. We live looking to the grace of Yeshua and the mercy of God. The mercy we have received from God must become mercy toward others.
If the Father has had compassion on us, we should have compassion on one another. If the Father has forgiven us, we should forgive one another.

What we know is partial. That is precisely why we need one another. The Church is not completed through the knowledge of one individual or the tradition of one denomination. We are different members of one body, and each member must strengthen the others through the gifts and understanding that God has given.

Therefore, the more we speak about the last days and the return of Yeshua, the more important it becomes not to calculate dates or obsess over the moment when we might be caught up, but to carry the cross entrusted to us today and follow Yeshua faithfully.
We should live each day seeking the grace and mercy of God, loving one another with the love with which the Father has loved us, showing compassion to one another, and forgiving one another.

All that we know is partial. That is why we need one another. May we not become people who judge and tear one another down, but members who build one another up, growing together in the Holy Spirit into the fullness of the body of Yeshua and faithfully walking the path entrusted to each of us as we await the Lord who is coming again. Amen.
